In [[probability theory]], '''Kemeny’s constant''' is the [[expected value|expected]] number of time steps required for a [[Markov chain]] to transition from a starting state ''i'' to a random destination state sampled from the Markov chain's stationary distribution.  Surprisingly, this quantity does not depend on which starting state ''i'' is chosen.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Crisostomi | first1 = E. | last2 = Kirkland | first2 = S. | last3 = Shorten | first3 = R. | doi = 10.1080/00207179.2011.568005 | title = A Google-like model of road network dynamics and its application to regulation and control | journal = International Journal of Control | volume = 84 | issue = 3 | pages = 633 | year = 2011 | bibcode = 2011IJC....84..633C }}</ref> It is in that sense a constant, although it is different for different Markov chains. When first published by [[John Kemeny (computer scientist)|John Kemeny]] in 1960 a prize was offered for an intuitive explanation as to why the quantity was constant.<ref name="kemeny">{{cite book | first1 = J. G. | last1 = Kemeny | author-link1 = John Kemeny (computer scientist) | first2 = J. L. | last2= Snell | author-link2 = J. Laurie Snell | title = Finite Markov Chains | location = Princeton, NJ | year = 1960 | publisher = D. Van Nostrand}} (Corollary 4.3.6)</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Catral | first1 = M. | last2 = Kirkland | first2 = S. J. | last3 = Neumann | first3 = M. | last4 = Sze | first4 = N.-S. | title = The Kemeny Constant for Finite Homogeneous Ergodic Markov Chains | doi = 10.1007/s10915-010-9382-1 | journal = [[Journal of Scientific Computing]] | volume = 45 | issue = 1–3 | pages = 151–166 | year = 2010 | url = http://www.hamilton.ie/skirkland/kemeny0209_revised.pdf| citeseerx = 10.1.1.295.9600 }}</ref> 

Beyond its theoretical importance, Kemeny’s constant is also applied in practice to evaluate the efficiency of robotic surveillance strategies. More precisely, Kemeny's constant measures how quickly a robot can navigate its environment using Markov chain-based methods.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=Weizhen |last2=He |first2=Jianping |last3=Duan |first3=Xiaoming |date=2024 |title=On the Trade-Off Between Efficiency and Unpredictability in Stochastic Robotic Surveillance |journal=IEEE Control Systems Letters |volume=8 |pages=2829–2834 |doi=10.1109/LCSYS.2024.3515858 |bibcode=2024ICSL....8.2829W |issn=2475-1456}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Patel |first1=Rushabh |last2=Agharkar |first2=Pushkarini |last3=Bullo |first3=Francesco |date=2015 |title=Robotic Surveillance and Markov Chains With Minimal Weighted Kemeny Constant |journal=IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control |volume=60 |issue=12 |pages=3156–3167 |doi=10.1109/TAC.2015.2426317 |bibcode=2015ITAC...60.3156P |issn=0018-9286}}</ref>

==Definition==

For a finite ergodic Markov chain<ref name="Levene">{{cite journal | last1 = Levene | first1 = Mark  | last2 = Loizou | first2 = George | year = 2002 | title = Kemeny's Constant and the Random Surfer | journal = The American Mathematical Monthly | volume = 109 | issue = 8 | pages = 741–745 | jstor = 3072398 | url = http://eprints.bbk.ac.uk/209/1/kemeny.pdf | doi=10.2307/3072398| citeseerx = 10.1.1.305.937  }}</ref> with [[Stochastic matrix|transition matrix]] ''P'' and invariant distribution ''π'', write ''m''<sub>''ij''</sub> for the mean first passage time from state ''i'' to state ''j'' (denoting the mean recurrence time for the case ''i''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''j''). Then
:<math>K = \sum_{j} \pi_j m_{ij}</math>
is a constant and not dependent on ''i''.<ref>{{cite journal|title=The Role of Kemeny's Constant in Properties of Markov Chains|first1=Jeffrey J.|last1=Hunter|year=2012|arxiv=1208.4716|doi=10.1080/03610926.2012.741742|volume=43|issue=7|journal=Communications in Statistics - Theory and Methods|pages=1309–1321}}</ref>
==Prize==

Kemeny wrote, (for ''i'' the starting state of the Markov chain) “A prize is offered for the first person to give an intuitively plausible reason for the above sum to be independent of&nbsp;''i''.”<ref name="kemeny" /> Grinstead and [[J. Laurie Snell|Snell]] offer an explanation by Peter Doyle as an exercise, with solution “he got it!”<ref>{{cite book | url = http://www.math.dartmouth.edu/~prob/prob/prob.pdf | first1 = Charles M. |last1 = Grinstead | first2 = J. Laurie | last2 = Snell | title = Introduction to Probability }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Two exercises on Kemeny's constant |url=http://www.math.uni-bielefeld.de/~souyang/OuyangTeaching2004/probintro/text/kc.pdf |url-status=usurped |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240131234651/https://sites.oxy.edu/lengyel/M372/papers/kc_PDoyle2005_KEMENY_CONSTANT.pdf |archive-date=31 January 2024 |access-date=1 March 2013}}</ref>
<blockquote>
In the course of a walk with Snell along Minnehaha Avenue in Minneapolis in the fall of 1983, Peter Doyle suggested the following explanation for the constancy of Kemeny's constant. Choose a target state according to the fixed vector '''w'''. Start from state ''i'' and wait until the time ''T'' that the target state occurs for the first time. Let ''K''<sub>''i''</sub> be the expected value of ''T''. Observe that
:<math>K_i+w_i \cdot 1/w_i = \sum_j P_{ij}K_j + 1</math>
and hence
:<math>K_i = \sum_j P_{ij}K_j.</math>
By the [[maximum principle]], ''K''<sub>''i''</sub> is a constant. Should Peter have been given the prize?
</blockquote>
